Problem Domain:
Public Health, Epidemiology, Spatiotemporal Data Analysis, Time Series Clustering, Machine Learning, Hierarchical Modeling.

Project Description:
This project develops a system to analyze nationwide epidemiological surveillance data (e.g., weekly incidence rates of a specific disease across multiple regions/states/counties). The primary goals are: 1) To identify distinct spatiotemporal patterns of disease spread by clustering regions based on their historical incidence time series using Pandas for data manipulation and Scikit-learn for clustering algorithms (potentially adapted for time series). 2) To visualize these patterns and cluster assignments effectively using Seaborn and potentially GeoPandas for map-based visualizations. 3) To build a predictive model using LightGBM, incorporating hierarchical features (e.g., national trends, regional averages) alongside local features, to forecast future outbreak risk (e.g., probability of exceeding a certain incidence threshold) at different geographical levels. The hierarchical modeling aspect aims to improve prediction accuracy by leveraging information from broader geographical contexts.

Frameworks Used:

  • Core Data: Pandas, NumPy
  • Machine Learning: Scikit-learn (Clustering: KMeans, DBSCAN, AgglomerativeClustering; Preprocessing: StandardScaler; Metrics; Model Selection: TimeSeriesSplit), LightGBM (Gradient Boosting Machine)
  • Time Series Specific: Statsmodels (e.g., for decomposition, autocorrelation features), potentially tslearn (for time series clustering metrics like DTW)
  • Visualization: Seaborn, Matplotlib
  • Geospatial (Optional but Recommended): GeoPandas (for spatial joins, map visualizations)
  • Configuration: YAML
  • Parallel Processing (Optional): Dask or Joblib (for speeding up clustering or feature engineering across many regions)

Dataset:
We will use publicly available data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). A good candidate is the weekly Influenza-Like Illness (ILI) surveillance data reported through FluView, which provides %ILI visits by HHS region and state.

  • Source: CDC FluView Portal (Data often available as downloadable CSVs).
  • Alternative: COVID-19 case/hospitalization data aggregated by state or county (e.g., from CDC COVID Data Tracker or sources like the New York Times dataset).
  • Geospatial Data: US Census Bureau shapefiles for states/counties (required for GeoPandas visualizations).

Use Cases:

  1. Pattern Identification: Discover groups of regions (states/counties) that exhibit similar temporal patterns of disease spread (e.g., early vs. late peaks, similar seasonality, rate of increase).
  2. Targeted Intervention Planning: Use cluster information to tailor public health interventions or resource allocation strategies to specific regional patterns.
  3. Outbreak Risk Forecasting: Predict the likelihood of future outbreaks or exceeding critical thresholds at state or potentially county levels, incorporating insights from regional/national trends (hierarchical aspect).
  4. Understanding Transmission Dynamics: Generate hypotheses about factors driving different spread patterns observed in clusters (e.g., demographics, climate, travel patterns, policy differences) for further investigation.
  5. Situational Awareness Dashboards: Visualize current epidemiological trends, cluster assignments, and outbreak predictions on maps and time series plots for public health officials.
  6. Comparative Analysis: Compare the epidemiological trajectory of a specific region to its cluster average or to other clusters.

Full Development Lifecycle (Corporate View):

  1. Problem Definition & Data Assessment (4-6 weeks): Define the specific disease(s), geographical scope (nationwide, specific states), temporal resolution (weekly, daily), prediction target (e.g., cases > X per 100k, % change > Y), and desired forecast horizon. Identify, access, and assess the quality/consistency of available epidemiological and relevant covariate data (e.g., demographics, mobility, vaccination rates).
  2. Data Ingestion & Preprocessing (6-10 weeks): Develop pipelines to reliably ingest data from sources (APIs, FTP sites, web scraping). Clean the data: handle missing values, correct reporting anomalies, standardize region names/codes. Aggregate/resample data to the desired temporal and spatial resolution. Merge with geospatial data.
  3. Feature Engineering (5-8 weeks): Create relevant features for clustering and prediction: lag features (incidence in previous weeks), rolling statistics (mean, std dev), time-based features (week of year, holidays), decomposition components (trend, seasonality from Statsmodels), potentially mobility data or weather data as external regressors.
  4. Time Series Clustering (6-9 weeks): Prepare time series data for clustering (e.g., normalize, extract shape features, use DTW distance). Apply clustering algorithms (KMeans, Agglomerative, DBSCAN) using appropriate distance metrics for time series (tslearn or custom features). Evaluate cluster quality (silhouette score, inertia, visual inspection). Assign cluster labels to each region.
  5. Hierarchical Model Development (8-12 weeks): Design the LightGBM model structure. Incorporate hierarchical features: e.g., add national average incidence, cluster average incidence, or state-level incidence as features when predicting for counties. Train LightGBM models, potentially one per cluster or a single model with cluster ID as a categorical feature. Perform hyperparameter tuning using time-series aware cross-validation (e.g., TimeSeriesSplit).
  6. Visualization & Interpretation (4-6 weeks): Develop visualizations using Seaborn and Matplotlib: plot time series for each cluster, show cluster assignments on a map (GeoPandas), plot feature importances from LightGBM. Interpret the identified patterns and model predictions.
  7. System Implementation & Validation (8-10 weeks): Build the end-to-end Python application integrating all steps. Implement robust validation strategies (temporal hold-out sets, potentially spatial cross-validation). Evaluate prediction performance using relevant metrics (RMSE, MAE, classification metrics if predicting thresholds).
  8. Deployment & Reporting (4-6 weeks): Package the application (e.g., Docker). Deploy to a suitable environment. Develop reporting mechanisms or dashboards (e.g., using Streamlit, Dash, or feeding results to BI tools) to communicate findings and forecasts.
  9. Monitoring & Retraining (Ongoing): Monitor data feeds for changes or quality issues. Monitor model performance over time. Implement scheduled retraining of clustering and prediction models as new data becomes available.

# --- Data Preparation ---
def pivot_data(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Pivots data to have regions as columns and dates as index."""
    try:
        df_pivot = df.pivot(index=DATE_COL, columns=REGION_COL, values=TARGET_COL)
        # Forward fill then backfill to handle missing values within time series
        df_pivot = df_pivot.ffill().bfill()
        # Ensure all columns are numeric
        for col in df_pivot.columns:
             df_pivot[col] = pd.to_numeric(df_pivot[col], errors=    coerce  )
        df_pivot = df_pivot.fillna(0) # Fill remaining NaNs (e.g., at start)
        logging.info(f"Pivoted data shape: {df_pivot.shape}")
        return df_pivot
    except Exception as e:
        logging.error(f"Failed to pivot data: {e}")
        raise

def engineer_features(df: pd.DataFrame, lags: List[int], window: int) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Engineers time series features for each region."""
    logging.info("Engineering features...")
    df_long = df.stack().reset_index().rename(columns={0: TARGET_COL})
    df_long = df_long.sort_values(by=[REGION_COL, DATE_COL])

    # Lag features
    for lag in lags:
        df_long[f"lag_{lag}"] = df_long.groupby(REGION_COL)[TARGET_COL].shift(lag)

    # Rolling features
    df_long[f"rolling_mean_{window}"] = df_long.groupby(REGION_COL)[TARGET_COL].shift(1).rolling(window=window, min_periods=1).mean()
    df_long[f"rolling_std_{window}"] = df_long.groupby(REGION_COL)[TARGET_COL].shift(1).rolling(window=window, min_periods=1).std()

    # Time features
    df_long["week_of_year"] = df_long[DATE_COL].dt.isocalendar().week.astype(int)
    df_long["month"] = df_long[DATE_COL].dt.month
    # df_long["year"] = df_long[DATE_COL].dt.year # Can cause issues if trend is strong

    # *** Pro Feature: Time Series Decomposition Features ***
    # Example using STL decomposition (Seasonal-Trend decomposition using Loess)
    # Requires running per time series, can be slow
    # grouped = df_long.set_index(DATE_COL).groupby(REGION_COL)[TARGET_COL]
    # trend_features = grouped.apply(lambda x: sm.tsa.seasonal_decompose(x, period=52, robust=True).trend if len(x)>104 else pd.Series(0, index=x.index))
    # seasonal_features = grouped.apply(lambda x: sm.tsa.seasonal_decompose(x, period=52, robust=True).seasonal if len(x)>104 else pd.Series(0, index=x.index))
    # df_long = df_long.merge(trend_features.rename(    trend   ), left_on=[REGION_COL, DATE_COL], right_index=True, how=   left    )
    # df_long = df_long.merge(seasonal_features.rename(    seasonal    ), left_on=[REGION_COL, DATE_COL], right_index=True, how=   left    )

    df_long = df_long.dropna() # Drop rows with NaNs created by lags/rolling
    logging.info(f"Feature engineering complete. Shape: {df_long.shape}")
    return df_long

# --- Clustering --- 
class TimeSeriesClusterer:
    def __init__(self, n_clusters: int = N_CLUSTERS, method: str =     kmeans  ):
        self.n_clusters = n_clusters
        self.method = method
        self.scaler = StandardScaler()
        self.model: Optional[Any] = None
        self.cluster_centers_: Optional[np.ndarray] = None
        logging.info(f"Initialized TimeSeriesClusterer with k={n_clusters}, method={method}")

    def fit(self, data_pivot: pd.DataFrame):
        """Fits the clustering model on the pivoted data."""
        # Data shape: (n_samples=n_regions, n_features=n_time_points)
        X = data_pivot.transpose().values
        logging.info(f"Clustering on data with shape: {X.shape}")

        # Scale features (time points)
        X_scaled = self.scaler.fit_transform(X)

        # *** Pro Feature: Use DTW with KMeans (requires tslearn) ***
        # if self.method ==     dtw_kmeans   and    tslearn  in sys.modules:
        #     logging.info("Using TimeSeriesKMeans with DTW...")
        #     # tslearn expects data in shape (n_samples, n_timestamps, n_features=1)
        #     X_ts = TimeSeriesScalerMeanVariance().fit_transform(X[:, :, np.newaxis])
        #     self.model = TimeSeriesKMeans(n_clusters=self.n_clusters, metric="dtw", max_iter=10, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)
        #     self.model.fit(X_ts)
        #     self.cluster_centers_ = self.model.cluster_centers_.squeeze() # Shape (k, n_timestamps)
        # elif self.method ==     kmeans  :

        if self.method ==     kmeans  :
            logging.info("Using standard KMeans on time points as features...")
            self.model = KMeans(n_clusters=self.n_clusters, random_state=42, n_init=10)
            self.model.fit(X_scaled)
            self.cluster_centers_ = self.scaler.inverse_transform(self.model.cluster_centers_) # Unscale centers
        elif self.method ==     agglomerative   :
            logging.info("Using Agglomerative Clustering...")
            # Linkage: ward, average, complete. Affinity: euclidean, cosine
            self.model = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=self.n_clusters, linkage=    ward    , affinity= euclidean   )
            self.model.fit(X_scaled)
            # Cannot easily get cluster centers for Agglomerative
            self.cluster_centers_ = None 
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"Unsupported clustering method: {self.method}")

        # Evaluate (optional)
        try:
             if hasattr(self.model,     labels_ ):
                 silhouette_avg = silhouette_score(X_scaled, self.model.labels_)
                 logging.info(f"Silhouette Score: {silhouette_avg:.4f}")
        except Exception as e:
             logging.warning(f"Could not calculate silhouette score: {e}")

    def predict(self, data_pivot: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.Series:
        """Assigns cluster labels to regions."""
        if self.model is None:
            raise RuntimeError("Clustering model not fitted yet.")
        X = data_pivot.transpose().values
        X_scaled = self.scaler.transform(X) # Use fitted scaler

        if hasattr(self.model,     predict ):
            labels = self.model.predict(X_scaled)
        elif hasattr(self.model,     labels_ ):
             # For models like Agglomerative fitted on the same data
             if X.shape[0] == len(self.model.labels_):
                 labels = self.model.labels_
             else:
                 raise RuntimeError("Cannot predict with Agglomerative on new data easily.")
        else:
             raise RuntimeError("Model does not support prediction or labels.")

        cluster_map = pd.Series(labels, index=data_pivot.columns, name=CLUSTER_COL)
        logging.info("Cluster assignments generated.")
        return cluster_map

# --- Hierarchical Prediction --- 
class HierarchicalPredictor:
    def __init__(self, model_params: Optional[Dict] = None):
        self.model_params = model_params if model_params else {
                objective   :   binary  , # Or  regression   depending on target
                metric  :   auc , # Or  rmse    ,   mae 
                n_estimators    : 1000,
                learning_rate   : 0.05,
                num_leaves  : 31,
                max_depth   : -1,
                feature_fraction    : 0.8,
                bagging_fraction    : 0.8,
                bagging_freq    : 1,
                verbose : -1,
                n_jobs  : -1,
                seed    : 42
        }
        self.model: Optional[lgb.LGBMClassifier] = None # Or LGBMRegressor
        self.features: List[str] = []
        logging.info("Initialized HierarchicalPredictor (LightGBM).")

    def _add_hierarchical_features(self, df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Adds features based on broader contexts (national, cluster)."""
        logging.info("Adding hierarchical features...")
        df_h = df.copy()
        # Ensure sorted by date for correct calculations
        df_h = df_h.sort_values(by=[DATE_COL, REGION_COL])

        # National average (excluding self?)
        df_h[    national_avg_incidence  ] = df_h.groupby(DATE_COL)[TARGET_COL].transform(   mean    )

        # Cluster average (if clusters assigned)
        if CLUSTER_COL in df_h.columns:
            df_h[    cluster_avg_incidence   ] = df_h.groupby([DATE_COL, CLUSTER_COL])[TARGET_COL].transform(    mean    )
            # Add cluster ID as categorical feature
            df_h[CLUSTER_COL] = df_h[CLUSTER_COL].astype(    category    )
        else:
             logging.warning("Cluster column not found, skipping cluster-level features.")

        # *** Pro Feature: State-level features if predicting for counties ***
        # if predicting for counties and state info is available:
        #    df_h[    state_avg_incidence ] = df_h.groupby([DATE_COL,     state_col   ])[TARGET_COL].transform(   mean    )

        # Lagged hierarchical features might also be useful
        df_h[    national_avg_lag_1  ] = df_h.groupby(REGION_COL)[   national_avg_incidence  ].shift(1)
        if CLUSTER_COL in df_h.columns:
             df_h[    cluster_avg_lag_1   ] = df_h.groupby(REGION_COL)[   cluster_avg_incidence   ].shift(1)

        # Drop rows with NaNs introduced by hierarchical feature lags
        df_h = df_h.dropna(subset=[    national_avg_lag_1  ] + ([  cluster_avg_lag_1   ] if CLUSTER_COL in df_h.columns else []))
        logging.info("Hierarchical features added.")
        return df_h

    def prepare_data_for_lgbm(self, df_featured: pd.DataFrame, horizon: int) -> Tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.Series, List[str]]:
        """Prepares data for LightGBM training, including target creation."""
        logging.info(f"Preparing data for LGBM with horizon {horizon}...")
        df_lgbm = df_featured.copy()

        # Create target variable: e.g., incidence `horizon` weeks ahead
        df_lgbm[    target  ] = df_lgbm.groupby(REGION_COL)[TARGET_COL].shift(-horizon)

        # If classification target: Predict if incidence exceeds threshold
        if self.model_params.get(    objective   ) ==    binary  :
             df_lgbm[    target  ] = (df_lgbm[   target  ] > LGBM_TARGET_THRESHOLD).astype(int)
             logging.info(f"Created binary classification target (incidence > {LGBM_TARGET_THRESHOLD})")
        else:
             logging.info("Created regression target (future incidence)")

        # Add hierarchical features
        df_lgbm = self._add_hierarchical_features(df_lgbm)

        # Drop rows where target is NaN (i.e., the last `horizon` rows for each group)
        df_lgbm = df_lgbm.dropna(subset=[    target  ])

        # Define features
        features = [col for col in df_lgbm.columns if col not in [TARGET_COL, DATE_COL, REGION_COL,     target  ]]
        # Ensure cluster ID is handled if present
        categorical_features = [CLUSTER_COL] if CLUSTER_COL in features else []
        features = [f for f in features if f != CLUSTER_COL or CLUSTER_COL not in categorical_features] # Keep non-cat features

        # Add back categorical feature name if it exists
        if categorical_features:
             features.extend(categorical_features)

        logging.info(f"Final features for LGBM ({len(features)}): {features}")
        logging.info(f"Categorical features: {categorical_features}")

        X = df_lgbm[features]
        y = df_lgbm[    target  ]
        self.features = features # Store feature names
        return X, y, categorical_features

    def train(self, X: pd.DataFrame, y: pd.Series, categorical_features: Optional[List[str]] = None, cv_splits: int = 5):
        """Trains the LightGBM model using TimeSeriesSplit cross-validation."""
        logging.info(f"Training LightGBM model with {cv_splits}-fold TimeSeriesSplit CV...")

        if self.model_params.get(    objective   ) ==    binary  :
            self.model = lgb.LGBMClassifier(**self.model_params)
        else:
            self.model = lgb.LGBMRegressor(**self.model_params)

        # TimeSeriesSplit for cross-validation
        tscv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=cv_splits)

        # Store OOF predictions and feature importances if needed
        oof_preds = np.zeros(len(X))
        importances = pd.DataFrame(index=self.features)

        # Convert categorical features for LGBM
        cat_feature_indices = [X.columns.get_loc(col) for col in categorical_features if col in X.columns]
        if cat_feature_indices:
             logging.info(f"Using categorical feature indices: {cat_feature_indices}")
             cat_feature_param = "auto"
             # Convert relevant columns to category type if not already
             for col in categorical_features:
                 if col in X.columns and X[col].dtype.name !=     category    :
                     X[col] = X[col].astype(    category    )
        else:
             cat_feature_param = None

        fold = 0
        for train_index, val_index in tscv.split(X):
            fold += 1
            logging.info(f"--- Training Fold {fold}/{cv_splits} ---")
            X_train, X_val = X.iloc[train_index], X.iloc[val_index]
            y_train, y_val = y.iloc[train_index], y.iloc[val_index]

            self.model.fit(X_train, y_train,
                           eval_set=[(X_val, y_val)],
                           eval_metric=self.model_params.get(    metric  ,   rmse    ),
                           callbacks=[lgb.early_stopping(100, verbose=False)],
                           categorical_feature=cat_feature_param)

            if self.model_params.get(    objective   ) ==    binary  :
                 preds = self.model.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1]
            else:
                 preds = self.model.predict(X_val)
            oof_preds[val_index] = preds
            importances[f    fold_{fold} ] = self.model.feature_importances_

        # Calculate overall OOF score (example: AUC for binary)
        if self.model_params.get(    objective   ) ==    binary  :
             oof_auc = sklearn.metrics.roc_auc_score(y, oof_preds)
             logging.info(f"Overall OOF AUC: {oof_auc:.4f}")
        else:
             oof_rmse = np.sqrt(sklearn.metrics.mean_squared_error(y, oof_preds))
             logging.info(f"Overall OOF RMSE: {oof_rmse:.4f}")

        # Retrain on full data
        logging.info("Retraining model on full data...")
        self.model.fit(X, y, categorical_feature=cat_feature_param)
        logging.info("Model training complete.")
        # Store average feature importance
        self.feature_importances_ = importances.mean(axis=1).sort_values(ascending=False)

    def predict(self, X: pd.DataFrame) -> np.ndarray:
        """Generates predictions on new data."""
        if self.model is None:
            raise RuntimeError("Model not trained yet.")
        logging.info(f"Generating predictions for {len(X)} samples...")
        # Ensure categorical features are handled correctly
        cat_feature_indices = [X.columns.get_loc(col) for col in self.features if X[col].dtype.name ==     category    ]
        if cat_feature_indices:
             for col in [X.columns[i] for i in cat_feature_indices]:
                 if X[col].dtype.name !=     category    :
                      X[col] = X[col].astype(    category    )

        if self.model_params.get(    objective   ) ==    binary  :
            return self.model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]
        else:
            return self.model.predict(X)

# --- Visualization --- 
def plot_clusters(data_pivot: pd.DataFrame, cluster_map: pd.Series, centers: Optional[np.ndarray]):
    logging.info("Plotting cluster time series...")
    n_clusters = cluster_map.nunique()
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(n_clusters, 1, figsize=(12, 3 * n_clusters), sharex=True)
    if n_clusters == 1: axes = [axes] # Make iterable if only one cluster

    for i in range(n_clusters):
        cluster_regions = cluster_map[cluster_map == i].index
        cluster_data = data_pivot[cluster_regions]
        axes[i].plot(cluster_data.index, cluster_data.values, color=    gray    , alpha=0.3)
        if centers is not None and i < len(centers):
             axes[i].plot(cluster_data.index, centers[i], color=    red , linewidth=2, label=f  Cluster {i} Center  )
        else:
             # Plot mean if centers not available (e.g., Agglomerative)
             axes[i].plot(cluster_data.index, cluster_data.mean(axis=1), color=    blue    , linewidth=2, label=f  Cluster {i} Mean    )
        axes[i].set_title(f"Cluster {i} ({len(cluster_regions)} regions)")
        axes[i].set_ylabel(TARGET_COL)
        axes[i].legend()
    plt.xlabel(DATE_COL)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

def plot_cluster_map(geo_data: gpd.GeoDataFrame, cluster_map: pd.Series):
    logging.info("Plotting cluster map...")
    if geo_data is None:
        logging.warning("Geo data not available, skipping map plot.")
        return
    try:
        # Merge cluster assignments with geo data
        geo_data_merged = geo_data.merge(cluster_map.reset_index(), on=REGION_COL, how="left")
        geo_data_merged[CLUSTER_COL] = geo_data_merged[CLUSTER_COL].astype(    category    )

        fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(15, 10))
        geo_data_merged.plot(column=CLUSTER_COL, categorical=True, legend=True,
                             ax=ax, missing_kwds={"color": "lightgrey", "label": "Missing/No Data"},
                             legend_kwds={    loc :   lower right })
        ax.set_title("Geographical Distribution of Clusters")
        ax.set_axis_off()
        plt.show()
    except Exception as e:
        logging.error(f"Failed to plot cluster map: {e}")

Where to Go From Here (Improvements):

  1. Advanced Clustering: Explore more sophisticated time series clustering algorithms (e.g., using shape-based features, autoencoders, or density-based methods like OPTICS adapted for time series). Evaluate different distance metrics (DTW, Euclidean on features, etc.).
  2. True Hierarchical Models: Implement statistically rigorous hierarchical models (e.g., Bayesian hierarchical models using Stan/PyMC, or specialized GBM packages that handle hierarchies explicitly) instead of just using hierarchical features.
  3. Geospatial Features: Incorporate spatial autocorrelation (e.g., using spatial lags calculated with GeoPandas/PySAL) or distance to neighbors as features in the prediction model.
  4. External Covariates: Integrate more external data relevant to disease spread (demographics, vaccination rates, mobility data, weather, policy changes) as regressors in the LightGBM model.
  5. Probabilistic Forecasting: Configure LightGBM (or use other models) to output probabilistic forecasts (quantiles or full distributions) instead of just point predictions or binary classifications, providing better uncertainty quantification.
  6. Dynamic Clustering: Implement methods to update cluster assignments dynamically as new data arrives, detecting when regions shift patterns.
  7. Causal Inference: Use techniques like causal forests or structural time series models to attempt to infer the causal impact of interventions or other factors on epidemiological trends, going beyond correlation.
  8. Scalability: For very high-resolution data (e.g., daily county-level), use Dask or Spark to parallelize feature engineering, clustering, and potentially model training.
  9. Ensemble Models: Combine predictions from LightGBM with other models (e.g., Prophet, ARIMA, deep learning models) to potentially improve robustness and accuracy.
  10. Interactive Dashboard: Build an interactive dashboard (e.g., using Dash or Streamlit) allowing users to explore clusters, view forecasts, and potentially simulate scenarios.
